speechtext:
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) gave me an indication during the question period that he would rise at three o'clock, and I see that he is rising now. The hon. member indicated that he would be raising a question of privilege because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) had said that he had misled the House. According to my recollection-and I have no notes to which I can refer- the minister, in answering the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, said that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby was wrong and that he should get his facts straight, or something to that effect.
I would indicate that a member is not entitled to enter into a dispute of this kind in this chamber. The minister did not say that the hon. member was misleading the House, nor that the hon. member had uttered a falsehood or anything of that nature which could lead us into some difficulty.
It seems to me that what has been said would provoke a debate between the two ministers. If the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby intends to develop a question of privilege, I would hope that it will be something more than simply challenging the minister about whether or not the hon. member was in error. Perhaps the hon. member will want to restudy his facts and check the record before carrying the matter further.
I will now hear the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby.

subtopic: PRIVILEGE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not need to check the record, but I will certainly respect your ruling. I would, very briefly, like to make my case.
I am sure that all members on this side have had encounters with the minister in which he has responded to questions in a way that the hon. member asking the question has no opportunity to reply. The minister leaves a clear impression that one is lying and that one is misleading the House by saying that the information which the hon. member has given in a question is false or wrong. Is the minister saying unequivocally that I am misleading the House, or would he, in support of his accusation, document very briefly his own case?
Politics ought to be about the application of certain principles. There should not be disagreement about the honesty of members in certain situations. If there is one member who is implying that the integrity of another member is not to be accepted, I think that that member should prove his case, and if he is wrong then he should be big enough to withdraw. If it is pointed out that I am incorrect, I will unequivocally admit that the minister is right, if he makes his case.
I was referring to three sets of figures. I used one set of figures in a question to the Minister of Employment and

The other figures to which I referred were taken from the minister's own document which he tabled in the House yesterday. It is the document which pertains to the National Plan of Action on the Status of Women. I said that there were 21 areas which were referred to for study, 15 for research, ten for examination and six for review. There were no figures for action. Mr. Speaker, I will try to be as brief as the hon. member. I stated that he was wrong on several counts. I can think of one in particular, which he did not repeat in his question of privilege, when he said that placement in the voluntary sector was being conducted at a cheaper cost than in the public sector by the Employment and Immigration Commission. For the record, I would like to point out to the hon. member that the specific case which he has brought before the House has an average placement cost of $324, that the average cost for placement per Outreach program is $112, and that unemployment and immigration placement costs $50. So the statement of the hon. member is completely wrong, completely erroneous. Whether or not he misled the House is a matter I will leave to him to decide. I say that he was wrong, and the facts that I have indicate that.
The hon. member then said that in the National Plan of Action there is no action now. I would like to point out to him for the record that the three changes which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) announced would take place are already in motion under this plan. With regard to unemployment insurance, supplementary unemployment benefit plans are extended to include plans covering unemployment costs as a result of maternity, paid maternity leave during the two-week waiting period would not affect UI benefits, payment of maternity benefits will be made outside Canada. We are working out the details of implementing this program.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, there is now before the House on the order paper a notice to introduce a bill amending the Criminal Code with regard to sexual offences. I have already indicated to the House the substance and the nature of those

changes which are being proposed. We are ready to move in these areas.
I could cite a number of other examples. We have announced that there will be a greater trades training program for women in non-traditional occupations right away. There will be greater accessibility to language training for immigrant women right away. There will be a greater amount of money allocated for research and information with regard to health and environmental issues particularly dealing with women. There will be priorities in these sectors. There will be a redirection of grants to labour organizations that will take place right away so as to encourage the support of women in the labour movement.
In terms of action which is presently taking place, I could go on. We are not talking about studies, reviews or anything of that nature, although, contrary to what the hon. member said, I do believe that a lot of issues need to be studied and examined. We do not necessarily have to decide policy by the seat of our pants, as the honourable member often does.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on what I think is perhaps one of the most basic questions of privilege that could ever be raised in this House. It is based on the fact that this institution is being used to create a false impression through the government's continued refusal or hesitation to make a reference to the appropriate committee of this House of the commodity tax review matter.
The reason I rise now is that, as I understand the government House leader's comments, he is now saying that while it is his intention to make a reference to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs with respect to this matter, he intends to delay it until the committee indicates that it is, in effect, ready for that reference.
The reason I rise on this question of privilege is that I feel there was a very important representation made in February to this House by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) when he gave 46 responses to the recommendations put forth by the so-called second tier committee dealing with task force reviews of various sectors of our industry.
Recommendation No. 6 of the second tier report dealt specifically with the federal sales tax matter. I should like to read verbatim the response of the government, which was as follows:
The Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has already received a large number of submissions on the report of the Commodity Tax Review Group. It is expected that the committee, after it has finished its review, will make recommendations on the structure of Canada's commodity tax system.
The important fact is that that committee has no reference. The commodity tax review group study is not before us. For months as members of that committee and in this House we have asked that the reference be made. I think it is important that the members of this House recognize that the government has represented to the outside world that a committee of this House is actively reviewing that study and will be, to use their words, making "recommendations on the structure of Canada's commodity tax system." It is doubly important when we bear in mind that we have just experienced the largest current account deficit in our history of $5.2 billion-

Mr. Speaker, two days ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) challenged me to set forth my views on what restrictions should be put on the use of social insurance numbers. Naturally I accept that challenge with great pleasure.
The purpose of this bill is to ensure that the use of social insurance numbers will not be expanded out of the original area for which they were brought in without first having prior consultation and full discussion in parliament on the subject, so that Canadians can have full participation and parliament can deal with this most important abuse in terms of individual privacy and human rights.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council) moved
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INDEPENDENCE OF PARLIAMENT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING CONFLICTS OF INTEREST
speechtext:
that Bill C-6, respecting the independence of Parliament and conflicts of interest of Senators and Members of the House of Commons and to amend certain other acts in relation thereto or in consequence thereof be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill represents extensive consultation with parliamentarians extending back more than five years. In July, 1973 I tabled a green paper entitled "Members of Parliament and Conflict of Interest". The proposals in that document received study by a committee of the House which reported in July of 1975, and by a committee of the Senate which reported in June of 1976.
The recommendations in those committee reports were given close consideration within the government, and in June of last year I introduced a bill entitled the Independence of Parliament Act and tabled a document setting out related proposals for changes to the rules of the Senate and the Standing Orders of the House. A bill incorporating some minor amendments has been reintroduced as Bill C-6, and the proposed Standing Orders have been again tabled without change. All members have now had the opportunity to review this bill and the proposed Standing Orders. I expect that hon. members would wish to give the bill second reading so that it would receive detailed consideration in the standing committee.
The principles underlying the proposed policy are straightforward, and the committees of both the House and the other place were in broad agreement with them. They are indeed the same principles that underscore statutes relating to standards of conduct of parliamentarians that date back to before confederation. As the title of the bill indicates, the main objective is to ensure that the independence of parliamentarians in the performance of their public duties is not affected by their private financial or professional interests. Members and senators are trustees of public confidence who must perform, and appear to perform, their duties in a manner reflecting the highest degree of concern for the public interest.
Both the public and parliamentarians, therefore, have an interest in a set of well defined standards. For the public, the conflict of interest rules will provide a clear assurance that the highest standards do prevail. For parliamentarians, the rules will make it easier to ensure that their activities conform to the ethical principles that the public has a right to demand.
Obviously setting clear standards is a complicated task. The rules must deal carefully and precisely with complex situations. There must be a fair balance between the requirements of sound conflict of interest provisions and the right of parliamentarians to manage their private affairs in ways that involve no threat to the public interest. The rules must be

March 8, 1979
Independence of Parliament
strong enough to merit public confidence without being so rigid and restrictive as to be unfair or to deter capable individuals from seeking public office.
It is also important to develop rules that do not unduly disadvantage any particular group. Members have very diverse professional backgrounds and financial interests; what would be an innocuous rule for one member could have very serious implications for another.
The proposed policy meets these challenges by combining the two basic approaches to dealing with potential conflicts of interest-disclosure and avoidance-and by providing the mechanisms through which parliamentarians can seek authoritative advice on the application of the policy. Much has been said about the respective merits of disclosure and avoidance. Each mechanism is apt in different circumstances and in meeting different needs.
Public disclosure of financial interests is a method of allowing members to continue managing their financial interests while at the same time making abuse of office less likely by allowing the public to judge their conduct in full knowledge of the facts. To put it another way, by allowing the public to know the facts the member is assured that what he does is subject to public scrutiny. Avoidance provisions are designed to prohibit parliamentarians from holding offices and managing financial assets which involve a conflict of interest or appear to create such a clear conflict.
Throughout the consultations and preparation of the policy, there has always been agreement that we should include both disclosure provisions and avoidance provisions. The strength of the policy lies in the way the two elements have been combined.
The bill requires parliamentarians to make very broad public disclosure of their assets, interests and activities. They will also have to make certain disclosures concerning interests of their spouses. Disclosure will be made annually through a registrar who will be an official of the House of Commons. It will include such major items as certain government contracts and grants; outside employment; gifts received by the parliamentarian or his or her spouse of a value greater than S100; honoraria; sponsored travel of the parliamentarian or his or her spouse outside Canada; real property of the parliamentarian or his or her spouse; shares and bonds of the parliamentarian or his or her spouse; unsecured debts over $5,000; trusts; and other sources of income worth more than $1,000. These are very significant disclosure requirements for members and also for the spouses.
The partial applicability to spouses reflects the need for another balance between conflicting objectives. On the one hand, there is the important principle that parliamentarians should not circumvent the rules through the activity of spouses. On the other hand, it is important not to restrict the ability of spouses to pursue independent careers. The bill resolves this quandary by requiring certain disclosures by spouses while exempting them from avoidance prohibitions. It is made clear, however, that parliamentarians may not escape

the avoidance provisions by asking their spouses to undertake prohibited activities on their behalf.
Another important feature of the disclosure provisions is that members and senators will be required to disclose any personal pecuniary interest they have in a matter when they are communicating with government bodies, public servants or other parliamentarians. This is to ensure that potential for a conflict of interest will be easily recognized by persons who may be in a position to make decisions affecting the interests of a parliamentarian.
The disclosure provisions simply require that a parliamentarian make public certain interests and activities. The avoidance provisions are more restrictive because they prohibit activities that either involve direct conflicts of interest or appear to involve conflicts. The prohibitions can be grouped under three main headings: prohibited fees; prohibited contracts and licences; and prohibited offices.
In the case of fees, parliamentarians will be prohibited from accepting compensation of any sort for interceding with other parliamentarians, public servants or government tribunals. They will also be prohibited from representing before these individuals and tribunals firms of which they are a director or officer. Finally, they will not be allowed to accept compensation for representing clients in court cases where the Crown in right of Canada is a party.
One of the most prominent areas for potential conflicts of interest is that of participation by parliamentarians in government contracts. The bill prohibits members and senators from being officers, directors, legal counsel, financial auditors or consultants for corporations that contract with or receive licences from the government. It also prohibits parliamentarians from holding significant share interests in such corporations.
The prohibitions should not restrict activity where there is little threat of a conflict between a parliamentarian's public duties and his or her private interests. For that reason, the bill contains a number of exemptions to the prohibition against participation in government contracts. 1 believe these exemptions will make good sense to both members and the public.
Parliamentarians will be permitted:
1.	To purchase government bonds or property, and to acquire permits where the terms are standard for all citizens;
2.	To hold publicly traded shares of corporations where he or she owns less than 5 per cent of $15,000 worth of voting shares;
3.	To participate in contracts authorized by the Government of Canada or parliament;
4.	To participate in government contracts where the aggregate amount is less than $1,000 in a given year.
Members will also be allowed to place their assets in trust if they do not wish to dispose of assets which might put them in
March 8, 1979

violation of the provisions of the act relating to prohibited contracts and regulated activities.
Thus, there will be a balance struck in the area of government contracts and licences. Contracts and interests will not be allowed where there is a recognizable potential for a conflict of interest, but they will be allowed where the potential for conflict is small. In the ordinary course of life members of parliament, like other citizens, will find it necessary to enter into contracts with the Government of Canada in ways which are not exactly obvious until one examines the question of government contracts more deeply.
The distinctions in the area of incompatible offices have been easier to draw. The bill states that parliamentarians will not be permitted to hold foreign, provincial or municipal offices, with few exceptions, or remunerated federal offices.
I need not describe in detail the administrative aspects of the bill. The basic approach is to place responsibility for the administration of the act in the Senate and the House of Commons. That responsibility will be exercised through standing committees of the Senate and the House and their registrars. Of course, the bill empowers only the courts to impose financial penalties for violations of the statute. The fact that a standing committee, for example, of this House can be established and will be involved in exercising the responsibility of carrying out the rules is not only an assurance that the standards will be maintained but also a protection to hon. members that, once having received the blessing or approval of certain activities or certain difficult borderline cases which might be dealt with by the committee, they need have no fear of legitimate public criticism of their activities.
It is my view, therefore, that although the introduction of a conflict of interest regime for members of parliament may appear demanding-and it is demanding-it is also a very desirable protection for them against unwarranted and unjustified criticism which may arise from time to time about their activities. They will, in a sense, be able to fall back on the prestige and authority of a standing committee of the House which will have the responsibility for the administration of the act.
As I said before, the conflict of interest policy proposed in this bill is a demanding one. However, it cannot and does not purport to deal with all ethical aspects of a parliamentarian's responsibility. To do this would lead to a code so detailed and complex that it would be unworkable and probably would obscure the main purpose of the policy. Certain principles cannot be codified into rules. Others need hardly be stated, such as a member's responsibility for the conduct of his staff and for the proper administration of the financial and other resources made available to him.
I would say that when hon. members begin to examine in detail the provisions of the bill they can undoubtedly point to various theoretical cases which could arise, and often it is difficult to devise precise guidelines for every foreseeable case. If we attempted to do so I think our task would be difficult indeed. But I think it is important that we have clear rules in
Independence of Parliament
order to maintain public confidence and for the protection of members from unfair criticism.
When discussing the question of conflict of interest, I have always said that while the rules, the legislation, the standards and the codes may be important, the fundamentally important matter is the moral commitment of members of the House of Commons.
It is my conclusion that the moral commitment of members of the House of Commons, by and large, is very high indeed and that in the pursuit of their activities they have been generally scrupulous in avoiding conflicts of interest; but while that may be the case, there will now be a code in operation which will make their obligations even clearer than they have been in the past. That is in a sense a benefit to members of parliament.
I believe we would all agree that the public has a right to expect the highest ethical standards of its representatives in parliament, and therefore we have a duty as members to leave the least possible doubt in that area. I believe this particular bill is a considerable attempt both to provide necessary guidelines for members of parliament and to provide them with protection against unjustified criticism. It will also be a considerable step in providing additional assurance to the public that members of parliament are conducting their affairs or their business with the public interest in mind and that their personal, professional and financial interests are not standing in the way of the carrying out of their public duties. That really is the purpose of this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to my colleague the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mac-Eachen), particularly to the last part of his speech when he went beyond the details or the framework of the bill and talked about the spirit of this legislation, and I want to assure him that that approach is also ours with respect to this legislation. That is why I think we all welcome the opportunity, after some period of time, to debate this legislation.
If we recall the time, the gestation period for this legislation is something like the gestation period leading to the birth of an elephant. It has been an extremely long period of time, especially when there has been such wide agreement on the necessity for legislation of this kind.
The green paper was tabled in July of 1973, almost six years ago. It was studied extensively by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and a substantial report was made on June 10, 1975. The proposals were also examined in the Senate in July of 1975 and, a year later, in July of 1976. Last June 26, as the minister has said, Bill C-62 was introduced, far too late to be passed in that session but perhaps not too late to be brought out if there was an election as evidence of the good intentions of the government.
Now we have Bill C-6, one of the first bills to be introduced in this session of parliament. I realize that time is always a

consideration, and in the normal event this will likely be one of the last bills to be brought forward in this parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INDEPENDENCE OF PARLIAMENT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING CONFLICTS OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Everyone's last expected date for an election call is really the Easter break, and that is what we are talking about, about mid-April. That seems to be the appropriate time. 1 cannot look into the mind of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) any more than can the Deputy Prime Minister. Unless the Prime Minister has taken leave of his senses, we will be into an election before any serious examination of this bill can be completed at all stages.
Today's debate will be brief. I will be the only speaker from this party. However, the committee discussions cannot be brief. Despite the agreement on principle which exists in the House, there are too many complex issues to be examined. Can we possibly cover all these issues adequately and appropriately in the spirit which was mentioned by the Deputy Prime Minister in the next three weeks, carry a report stage and third reading and then get the bill through the Senate, which has a great and legitimate interest in its provisions? I suspect not. Even if we could, the question is, can the Chief Electoral Officer put into place the sections on declarations to returning officers?
It is not hard to conclude that this bill is being dragged out for the second time on the eve of an election as a campaign ploy and that this debate is all fanfare and no parade. If the government really wanted this bill through and in place on the statute books, it would have proceeded with it back in October, November or perhaps December.
I must also express my disappointment that the codification of conflict of interest laws has not been done comprehensively to include cabinet ministers as a separate category, and public servants as well. It seems that members of parliament, who are generally perceived as the least powerful element in the governmental process-nonentities, or "nobodies" in the words of the Prime Minister-are singled out first so that they do not abuse the power this government has never let them have. I think we have our priorities mixed in terms of where the legislative structure on conflict of interest should begin. I think it would have been more appropriate to spell out conflict of interest rules for members of parliament in the first part of the

bill and then to add a second part with even stricter rules for cabinet ministers and public servants.
Be that as it may, conflict of interest rules are necessary and welcome, and if this bill is not passed before the election is called a Progressive Conservative government will bring in one at least as strong.
The reasons for this bill are fairly clear. As government- lamentably in some instances-extends its control over all types of business and other activities in this country, the possibility that a member of parliament or a group of members of parliament may be affected directly by an item of legislation, a regulation or some other government action brought before the House increases. We have to recognize that, and we have to ensure that discussions are undertaken to determine what is in the national interest, without distortions caused by conflict of interest in the House itself. Members have to draw a line between, on the one hand, representing their communities or interests with which they are familiar and, on the other hand, representing themselves. I suppose that is the nub of the problem which this bill seeks to address. I do believe that this is not yet a frequent occurence, as the Deputy Prime Minister said. We are, rather, anticipating and meeting a danger which has not yet reached the critical point.
More important for the moment than clear and present instances among members of parliament of conflict of interests is a strong public perception that the danger is not in the future but in the present. We have to take cognizance of that public perception. It is a feature of our national political environment that we do not function in isolation from events in other jurisdictions. The common political gossip of our news media is drawn from the entire democratic world. If an American senator appears to have misappropriated public funds or succumbed to a bribe, that is on our front pages in Canada and it reflects on all of us who are in the legislative function.
When a British member of parliament goes for a swim in Florida and reappears in Australia-and we had an instance of that-we are as fascinated by that as are his own electors. The word "Watergate" conveys almost as rich and varied a meaning to us in Canada as it does to the Americans when they consider their own jurisdiction. These events, however little they may be drawn from our own experience, are a part of our environment and the climate of distrust which appears to go automatically with democratic politics, particularly in those societies which began their political systems when the country was an underdeveloped frontier area.
Sadly, not all blame for the poor image of politicians can be shifted to other countries. We are not free of clear instances of unwarranted use of influence on the part of politicians and their close associates. In the recent past, three of our colleagues have, regrettably, been involved with the courts on charges not reflecting on the dignity or propriety of this House. If we wish to be free of all suspicion, we must be clear of all charges. If we wish to establish and to continue the trust
March 8, 1979

we feel we deserve, there is absolutely no alternative to the passage of strict conflict of interest rules as quickly as possible.
In examining Bill C-6 we must remember that nothing in a political system happens in isolation, and I think this is the point which the Deputy Prime Minister was trying to make. We are all aware that nothing worth while can be accomplished without significant consequences, both intended and unintended. We want to make sure that anyone who is elected to this House is encouraged to uphold its reputation for impartiality. Equally, we do not want to turn away people who should be here. Every decision we make in the House about salary, staff and rules of behaviour affects the type of membership we will have.
Conflict of interest rules must be carefully designed to fulfil their purpose without the unwarranted side effect of discouraging from public duty anyone who has been successful in his career as an independent businessman, a professional, a skilled tradesman or a farmer. It will be of little utility to the reputation and representative quality of this House if it were to be filled entirely with former salaried employees. This will be the challenge of the committee study-to ensure that this bill is clear, fair and enforceable, without making it a barrier over which the most talented in our society cannot leap.
To retain its full vigour and relevance we must continue to attract to the House of Commons men and women at the peak of their energy and creativity. We must remember too that not everyone elected to the House is able to remain as long as he or she might wish.
I hope that when this bill goes to committee we will be given a clear idea of the type of regulations contemplated for it. As well, it would be useful to hear a little more about clause 2(2), which seems to contemplate "any decision, order, rule or regulation" being overturned by the House, without spelling out exactly how this is to be done. To leave it too vague is to put the procedure for even initiating such a reconsideration entirely at the discretion of the cabinet, and none of us wants that to happen regardless of the political stripe of the cabinet.
Several of the provisions of this bill have been designed-I say this with some regret-without sufficient consideration of the fact that the House is a political forum, the actions of which in many cases are in fact the actions of the majority only. For this reason, they seem to me to provide insufficient protection for the minority opposition parties in the House.
When a candidate is running for election, he or she must make a statement to the deputy returning officer, who happens to be a government appointment, whatever the government is, and partisan favouritism has been known to be a factor. The registrar described in the bill is appointed by the cabinet. Everyone knows that this government would never appoint a Liberal partisan to such a position-we know they do not do that kind of thing, especially in the case of a position for which he might be entirely unsuited-but some future government might, and we must guard against the actions of future governments.
Independence of Parliament
I am glad to see members on the other side and perhaps to my left, when contemplating a future government, looking to this side of the House. I think that is very encouraging. Pity the poor opposition spokesman-and my friend might very well have to consider that situation-who has had to bare his soul to a local government appointee, fly to Ottawa on "Air Mackasey," and then put himself at the mercy of a government appointed registrar. If a member is appealing for some sort of exemption or judgment before the committee established by the draft Standing Orders which will be sent to the standing committee for consideration with this bill, he would undoubtedly feel slightly uncomfortable laying out his case before a committee that happens to be controlled by his opponents.
The situation is a difficult one. Would it not be tempting in some situations to knock off a few troublesome opposition members of parliament by making life unusually difficult for them under the conflict of interest rules and by refusing normal and reasonable exemptions? That is a possibility which we have to consider.

speechtext: It may be very shortsighted.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INDEPENDENCE OF PARLIAMENT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING CONFLICTS OF INTEREST
speechtext:
I do not want to be partisan with respect to this matter, but this government and other governments have been known to do things from time to time that are very shortsighted. I call them lapses of judgment, but they do lessen the opportunities for the House to be as representative as possible; and with the possibility of that happening-I think we should be on our guard and devise ways of getting around it. It is a situation which I think deserves the best from all of us.
The whole set-up is itself a conflict of interest between the obligation to treat all members alike and the demands and emotions of partisan competition. That is why I think it would not be unreasonable for the committee to consider some changes, perhaps one where candidates should make declarations to the Chief Electoral Officer rather than to the returning officer in each of the ridings. That would remove it from the passionate political atmosphere. The registrar should be appointed after consultation with and approval by all parties- that is not in the bill but it would be an improvement to the legislation-and after passage of a debatable motion in the House. The position of registrar is so important to the working of the bill that it should not be merely left to the judgment of the cabinet. I think it should be left at least to the judgment of and consideration by the House in the way in which I suggest.
Any committee that is established should not operate on the basis of a simple majority. That is built into the bill now. There is a potential for unfairness. We should consider other methods of getting around that so that the committee can function on some basis other than a simple majority. Because it is a unique committee and may require unique ground rules. Perhaps in doing that we should consider whether some special protection for minority party members of parliament should be built into that structure. Those are matters to which we would like to have attention directed.

March 8, 1979
Independence of Parliament
1 remind hon. members that until the passage of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act the setting of boundaries for redistribution was under the control of the House itself. The situation led us directly to abuses and a new system had to be introduced. In respect of the matter I have been speaking about, there are in this bill many features that smack of the worst abuses of the old redistribution mechanism which I think should be removed or tempered. I do not think we ought to put ourselves in the position with this important bill where we have to re-learn a lot of old lessons which I think are better behind us than in front of us.
Many features of the bill are quite satisfactory and I am pleased to see the comprehensive nature of the disclosure which must be made. We have regarded in the past and are continuing to regard in the future such things as speaking engagements as part of our public duty. As MPs we are all supposed to discuss political issues with the public and to hear their views. This duty should not be regarded as an opportunity for profit. I think disclosure will help prevent that.
So far this temptation has not been too strong for members of this House, and it is not likely to become strong because I do not think we are seen by the public as entertaining personalities to the extent that perhaps some of our friends in the free world are seen as entertaining personalities, people who are paid huge honorariums for speaking. Indeed, the United States is one of those jurisdictions where that has taken place and the congress there has moved against it. They have used their methods, and this is one way that we are considering in moving against that kind of thing in this country.
The touchier issue of foreign travel is also included. We have in the past in this House left this to individual consciences and justification. What I am talking about when I refer to foreign travel is travel by a member of parliament at the expense of a foreign government. My own party has actively discouraged the acceptance of such foreign-paid trips. There is no doubt that foreign countries offer such trips to members of parliament to influence them, and our position is not strong if we are reduced to arguing whether these generous hosts receive value for the money. It is not an argument we ought to enter into. It is a good thing that this bill lays it out clearly that this is a matter to be disclosed.
Another provision the committee will have to look at, and which bothers me a good bit, is clause 23 which specifies that the Statutory Instruments Act does not apply to regulations made by the designating committee under this act. I happen to be a member of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who is in the House today, is co-chairman of that committee. We are developing and have developed guidelines by that statute for a review of statutory instruments such as orders in council and other things, work that I consider to be quite important. As time goes on that work will grow in importance, in an era when the government seems to step more and more into areas where it heretofore had not trodden. I do not see why that act ought not to apply to statutory instru-

ments which arise from this statute. I know it may not be desirable to have one committee reviewing the work of another, but I think we should retain this control over the possibility of abuse of regulatory power.
I have tried to be brief, but I want to say in conclusion to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my colleague the government House leader, that we approve of the principle of this bill and most of its detail. I am sorry there is not more of it and that it did not come sooner so the committee would have the realistic hope of finishing its work. The government should have given us a bill that covered all possible instances of conflict of interest. Indeed, there has been time for that over the period of years about which I spoke earlier, but the government has chosen not to do that. It has chosen this first step at the beginning to give us a bill in areas which so far have caused us the least trouble.
I have indicated that we favour the principle of the bill and there will be no other speaker from our party for that reason. We are anxious to get this bill to the committee because it is important not only that this House operates appropriately, not only that members conduct themselves appropriately, but that this parliament-not just this House but as well the other chamber-appear to operate and act appropriately, and that the respective members of each of our Houses appear to act the same way.
It is in that spirit that we accept this bill for the purpose of getting it to the committee where it can be dealt with, and we are anxious to deal as expeditiously as we can in the circumstances with all its detail. We shall be suggesting some changes to strengthen the bill along the lines proposed by the government.

He was acting as prime ministers do in that situation, talking without giving any precise answer.
I believe the Prime Minister made one thing very clear, and that is that he does not intend to exceed the length of time set by two procedents, and he referred by name to Prime Minister Bennett and Prime Minister Mackenzie King. We know in the case of Prime Minister Bennett that he called the election in 1935 for a date that was five years and three months after the one that had been held in 1930. We know in the case of Prime Minister Mackenzie King that he called the election in 1945, so that it was held five years and three months after the one that had been held in 1940. Whatever else the present Prime Minister said last night, he made it pretty clear that he would not exceed those precedents. speechtext:
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, this little by-play in which we are indulging is intended to underline the fact that there could be time, not just for today's second reading debate but for this piece of legislation, to be dealt with in committee, reported back to the House and for the government House leader to call it. It is an important piece of legislation dealing with a very important subject.
This is not the first time that we have had legislation dealing with the independence of parliament. There are a number of sections in the Senate and House of Commons Act, sections 10 to 24 inclusive, which have the general heading, "Independence of Parliament", and there are also three sections- sections 3, 4 and 5-in the House of Commons Act which relate to the independence of parliament.
A great deal has happened in society and things have become a great deal more complex and much more involved than they were in the days when those pieces of legislation were passed, however, and it is certainly time that our conflict of interest legislation as it affects members of parliament should be brought up to date. That is the purpose of this legislation.
As the government House leader pointed out, the matter has been discussed previously in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, and there was general agreement in that committee on the main outlines of the bill which is now before us. I think that it is reasonable to hope, if the committee has a bit of time to deal with the bill, that it might make a few amendments, some of which I think are desirable, and that it get the bill back in time to be passed before this session ends.
My friend from Grenville-Carleton wondered what the Chief Electoral Officer would do if a bill which includes amendments to the Canada Elections Act were passed very close to the election. I would point out to him, of course, that even the passing of the bill would not put it into effect. It comes into effect at a date to be fixed by proclamation. Even if we had the bill on the statute books, the government could delay proclamation until after the election. Then, of course, it would be up to whatever group of men and women who form the government at that time to decide what to do about the matter.
I think that most of us agreed with the general principles that were outlined by the Deputy Prime Minister when he made his statement introducing the bill today, and it is not necessary to go over that ground. The Deputy Prime Minister made reference to the fact that any bill-and this bill is one in point-that lays down rules regarding one's holdings, investments or connections can be awkward for some persons either in this House or in the other place. There is no use denying that. But I make again the point, which I think my hon. friend across the way made and which the hon member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) made, namely, that the public interest

March 8, 1979
Independence of Parliament
comes first. If it is a bit awkward for some members to have to declare their holdings and their interest, the fact that the public interest comes first overrides that awkwardness.
I appreciate the fact that the legislation deals with two main areas. There is the area of avoidance which informs members of parliament and senators of the kinds of things they must avoid. The other area is disclosure. The bill does not say that a member cannot have investments, resources or what have you, but the heart of the legislation is that there shall be full and complete disclosure. I hope that there are no loopholes in this bill that would make it possible for members of parliament or senators to avoid that requirement of complete disclosure. Sometimes I wonder about this business of a blind trust. I think that the committe had better take another look at that. One wonders at times whether that is not a means of avoiding the real intent of legislation.
1 would like to support the point made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton with regard to the registrar. We already have certain officers who are regarded as officers of parliament. 1 refer to the Chief Electoral Officer, the Auditor General and the Commissioner of Official Languages. There may be one or two others, but certainly those three are regarded as officers of parliament. It may be that the government makes the choice and the nomination, but at least the matter must come before parliament and be the subject of a resolution of the House of Commons.
It would seem to me that that type of position ought to apply in the case of the registrar for both Houses or one registrar for each House. I suppose that I might go so far as to let the senators in the other place have a say about their registrar. I am not sure though; it is someting that I will have to think about.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

I feel that it does make a difference and is more than just so many words for an officer to be appointed by a resolution of this House rather than by the governor in council. The governor in council appointment means that it is cabinet appointment exclusively, and that we learn about the appointment afterwards. If it were to be an officer approved by the House of Commons, at least we would be told in advance and at least there would be some consultation and assurance that the person proposed is acceptable to all parties in the House. I would urge that that change at least be made in the bill when it gets into the hands of the committee.
There is one aspect of this whole situation that still worries some of us. I am referring to the special position of cabinet ministers. I know that the government's argument in presenting this legislation is that by laying down rules that apply equally to all members of parliament, whichever House they are in, cover cabinet ministers because cabinet ministers are either in this House or over in the other place.
However, cabinet ministers have a special position in that they know what is going on more than some of the rest of us. They are involved in deals and contracts of one kind or

another. I do not wish to make reference to any names, but it does concern us at times when a person who has been a cabinet minister leaves this place and in the course of a very short time turns up on the board of directors of some giant corporation which, in turn, deals with the government. That kind of situation ought to be covered somewhere in the legislation.
I know that even before this bill was presented, the Prime Minister established a kind of voluntary registry for cabinet ministers, and under certain conditions one can find the information therein, but there is no legislation requiring such disclosure. There are certain rules of conduct or guidelines about what ministers can do within a period of time after they leave a cabinet post, but they are only guidelines. They do not have the force of legislation. I think they should and I think they ought to be in this particular act that is before us now. I urge that when the committee is dealing with this bill clause by clause it consider this point.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton had quite a bit to say about the public's view of politicians. Whatever happens to a politician anywhere in the world, and certainly in the democratic world, seems to reflect on us in this country. That puts a pretty heavy responsibility on us to be above reproach in every possible respect. I suggest that means we have to think very carefully about the things we do, not only with respect to legislation, contracts and all the rest, but about the things we do for ourselves.
I am not going to get into a long speech on a subject about which I feel very strongly, but I hope that in the next parliament we will think very carefully about what we do with respect to pay, allowances, trips, perquisites and all the rest for members of parliament. I do not think it would hurt us to have to struggle a bit to do our job instead of taking the position that we have to be well taken care of. That is not something to be put into this kind of legislation, but if we want to convince the people out there that we mean it when we say we require integrity, honesty and dependability on the part of members of parliament, we should go all the way with it.
I indicated at the start that on this side of the House we gave our agreement that there would be a short debate-one speaker per party-to let the bill go to committee. With that there was also a commitment that our speeches would not be long. I am happy to say that we are prepared to give this bill second reading this afternoon. We hope the government House leader will show that it is not just a piece of window-dressing, but that he is serious about it and will put it pretty close to the top of the list-right up there with veterans affairs as something to be dealt with before this session ends.

subtopic: DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-35, an act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto.
As members of the House are aware, when this bill was introduced for second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, speakers on this side indicated that we were in agreement with the government's proposal to set up a department of fisheries and a separate department of the environment. In our opinion the government should not have divided the two responsibilities in 1970. It was not long after the change was made that the government realized that it had made yet another blunder and it has taken approximately nine years to right the wrong that was committed in 1970.
During second reading debate we also suggested the bill be sent to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry rather than to the miscellaneous estimates committee. The government accepted this proposal. The fact that the bill is back in the House this afternoon is indicative that we made a sound recommendation. It is unfortunate the government does not follow the sound advice we give it more often.
Quite frankly, the bill would have been returned to the House at an earlier date if the minister and government supporters had been more co-operative. When the bill was under discussion in committee we raised no objections to the minister reading a lengthy statement dealing with it and other matters pertaining to the over-all fishing industry. However, this co-operation unfortunately was not in evidence when members of the opposition asked relevant questions relating to policies of the new department. It was only after members of the opposition, following an hour and a half of stonewall tactics, walked out of the committee-the minister laughs, Mr. Speaker. These are the facts as I recall them. The minister sat there and said nothing. All he had to do at that time was say- and he was surrounded by his officials-that he had no objection to members of the opposition asking questions. However, that reasonable course was not followed, and it was only after we walked out of the committee en masse that they relented, which resulted in the bill finally being passed. But the government's actions did delay study of the bill.

March 8, 1979
Government Organization
When making this strict ruling initially we wondered what the government had to hide. This soon became evident. It had given windfall profits to certain fish companies and processors by allocating quotas to them which they could in turn sell to foreigners. According to statements made by the minister and the government's supporters, this policy did cost Canada some jobs. It also became clear that Canada has been out-negotiated by the United States in the quota allocations on Georges Bank.
In addition, as has happened in so many other areas, the government appears to have adopted a policy which we on this side put forth, namely that of licensing at least five freezer trawlers over a five-year period to catch species which Canadians have not generally fished. This is evident in the decision to allow Canadians to catch loligo squid in the U.S. fishing limit zone. I point out to the House that squid has to be frozen almost immediately it is brought in from the ocean so as to retain its quality.
During our examination of the bill a number of government amendments were moved, primarily to improve the French text. It is a matter of some regret, however, that I say to you, sir, and inform the House that an amendment moved by the official opposition to strengthen the proposed fisheries and oceans research advisory council was rejected by government supporters. As the bill reads at present, the government proposes to set up an advisory council under the control of the minister which shall consist of a chairman and not more than 24 other members. It is proposed that members of the council shall include persons from departments, boards and agencies of the Government of Canada.
At that point it was proposed by supporters of the official opposition that the advisory council also contain members representing governments of consenting provinces, for example, those that have a specialized interest in the marine sciences. Unfortunately, this worth-while proposal, which we believe would have served to give the provinces a sense of belonging, a sense of making a contribution, a feeling of unity and of participation in helping solve some of the very basic problems troubling the fishing industry on both coasts, was rejected by government supporters.
Undoubtedly there are times when it is necessary to be partisan, but there are other times when I believe a government should be conciliatory and not reject a worth-while proposal just because it comes from supporters of the official opposition. In my view, this was one of those occasions when the government should have considered some provincial representation on the research advisory council. Such a move would have strengthened the work of the council, and though we in the opposition believe that the over-all management of our fisheries resources must remain in the hands of the federal government, we also believe that there is a greater need for consultation with provincial fisheries ministers concerning the manner in which quotas are established and the manner in which these quotas are allocated to the provinces concerned and to foreign countries fishing within our 200-mile zone.
We in the official opposition believe that the role of the province must be strengthened so they can assist in upgrading

the present processing facilities within their borders. Still more emphasis must be placed on upgrading the quality of our fisheries products if we hope to make further inroads into the American market. This is equally true, sir, if we hope to make a dent in the European Economic Community.
At the present time there is great uncertainty within the industry over our future prospects in Europe due, in no small measure, to this government's close-mouthed approach to the GATT negotiations. Since 1974 the industry has submitted three briefs to the Canadian trade and tariffs committee. However, there has been little by way of communication between the government and the industry about progress in the negotiations. At one time, prior to Britain joining the European Economic Community, Canada had free entry of canned salmon, shrimp and lobster into the British market. Now the tariffs on these products range from 17 per cent to 18 per cent, despite the fact that these tariffs are not protecting any European product. The same tariff walls apply to groundfish where exports to the Common Market face a tariff of some 15 per cent to 18 per cent, whereas the Common Market tariff against Norwegian groundfish exports is something like 3 per cent, and I believe Iceland exports its groundfish into the European Economic Community duty free.
The Canadian fishing industry in particular seeks only equal treatment with its two main competitors. It continues to ask just what is going on with the GATT negotiations. I ask the government, what does it have to hide? Why is the government so secretive about the progress, or perhaps I should say the lack of progress, that is being made behind closed doors? I submit you could get more information about the GATT negotiations from the Kremlin than from this government. It is high time that our negotiators and representatives pointed out to these countries that Canada is still granting licences allowing them to fish within our waters. Surely one favour deserves another.
Last year-the minister can correct me if I am wrong but I obtained these figures from the minister's officials in Halifax and I presume them to be correct-we licensed some 300 foreign freezer trawlers and some 190 foreign factory ships which enabled them to carry out fishing operations within our 200-mile limit. Surely this is worth something in the way of a negotiating tool when one sits down with European friends and discusses trade. The fishing industry is not asking for special concessions; it is asking for an equal opportunity when trying to make sales to the European Economic Community.
We asked that the provinces be represented on the advisory council, for we believe they should have the right to make a greater input into the field of fisheries research. The minister has cut down on the number of scientists employed on the east and west coast. I will not quibble with him over the numbers but my information is that some 34 scientists have been laid off, some 23 on the east coast and 11 on the west coast. These men will no longer be employed in the department. All of this is happening at a time when we have declared a 200-mile limit, when the need for specialized research in the fishing industry was never greater.
March 8, 1979

The provincial arm in this field should be strengthened. In fact, that was the interpretation I took from the minister's remarks when we discussed this issue on previous occasions. In my opinion and the opinion of my party, the place to start this form of meaningful discussion would be with the fisheries and oceans research advisory council. We also believe that the provinces should be represented on the advisory council, which is Part II of Bill C-35, because the province should have their hands strangthened in the field of fisheries education.
There are vast changes taking place in the fishing industry today. New species are being utilized; the catching of capeling, although the stocks are declining, the catching of squid, silver hake, round-nosed grenadier, to name but a few. These are all specialized species, fish that we have not previously utilized because the regular groundfish species, namely cod, haddock, hake and pollack, to name but a few, were in plentiful supply. Now we are aware that some countries look upon some of these species as a delicacy. Squid in particular are considered a delicacy by Japanese interests. Therefore, we believe that new emphasis must be placed on the scientific as well as the educational end of the fishing industry. Our fishermen must be trained in these new techniques.
In the view of the official opposition, this should be the role filled by the provinces. The provincial administrations are closer to the resource, certainly closer than is Ottawa. They are more aware of the species and the methods that must be used in catching them.
These are at least three fields where greater authority can be vested in the provinces. We believe that if this course is followed, our fishermen, whether they be inshore, mid-water or offshore, will enjoy even greater opportunities in this important primary industry.
There is room for hope as evidenced in clause 6 of the bill, which states that the minister of fisheries and oceans may enter into agreements with the government of any province or any agency thereof respecting the carrying out of programs for which the minister is responsible.
This section raises a number of important questions. For example, on February 14 the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) made a statement outside the House which was really a carbon copy of the releases made by his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), dealing with the agreement reached between Canada and the United States for the Atlantic coast fisheries and boundaries disputes.
In the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs we are told that the two treaties, the one on the third party settlement of the boundary and the other on fisheries arrangements, will be completed and ready for signature, if possible, by the beginning of March. I would like to know whether these treaties have been signed. Why were these statements made outside the House? Who determined these quotas and the species to be caught in various areas? What
Government Organization
fisheries groups were consulted prior to these decisions being taken by our Canadian negotiator?
Were the provincial fisheries ministers consulted on this matter? Will there be any opportunity provided for members of parliament from all parties for an in depth study and debate on this important matter? Speaking of boundaries, where do we stand in our negotiations with France over the fisheries and boundaries claims put forth by France around the small islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon?
When speaking about agreements with the provinces as outlined in Bill C-35, I cannot help but ask what happened to federal-provincial negotiations when the minister recently awarded contracts for the catching of 12,000 tons of codfish off the coast of Labrador. The manner in which the minister awarded each of the five eastern provinces a share of this catch has created considerable concern in all areas, especially among Canadian fishermen. To help clear up this confusion, I believe it would be beneficial if the minister informed us about the method he used to determine the foreign countries that would be licensed to catch these fish, the method used for determining the quotas to be awarded to each province and the final disposition of the processed product. Just what are the terms of the contract he arranged with two communist countries, East Germany and Poland, and how much provincial input was obtained prior to making these decisions so vital to the people of Atlantic Canada?
According to all reports, inshore fishermen are dissatisfied with the government's policy as it applies to class A lobster licences. They claim that present regulations are defeating the idea of a multipurpose inshore fishery. This is especially true in the Northumberland Strait area where a recent meeting was held between the district protection officer and some 70 fishermen who stated that class A licence holders should be allowed to fish for anything available.
These same fishermen have stated that they are also unhappy with the present government's policy on scallop licences. Current regulations state that only those who took scallop during the last two years will be eligible for a licence this year. In addition, the area manager for fisheries has also stated that anyone who has not been active in the groundfish industry will get a licence this year.
Here we have three distinct problems all dealing with licences, licences of lobsters, scallop and groundfish which are requested by our inshore fishermen. I hope the minister will explain the rationale behind his present policies which are obviously creating mistrust and frustration among the inshore fishery of this area.
When we raise these issues, government supporters often ask what we would do. They say it is easy for us to criticize. There are at least 18 different species of clawed lobsters in the Atlantic ocean and another 12 from the Indian and Pacific oceans. Since all clawed lobster species other than Canadian, American and European live in relatively deep water, there has been little commercial development except for the Norway lobster whose current landings exceed the combined catch of European and Canadian and American lobsters.

March 8, 1979
Adjournment Motion
In the Atlantic ocean clawed lobsters occur from Greenland and Iceland south to the waters southeast of the Falkland Islands and the southern tip of South America. One species has been reported from deep water off New Jersey down through the Caribbean with additional species also in the Gulf of Mexico.
Although most clawed lobsters are much smaller than the Canadian-American and European lobsters, many of them compare in size with the canning lobsters of the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence, approximately two and three quarter inches in carapace length.
It is my understanding that Norwegian clawed lobsters prefer colder temperatures than the European or Canadian-American lobster. Has the minister ever considered conducting experiments which might lead to establishing the Norway lobsters in our own habitat, closer to the Atlantic coast, which would be beneficial to our inshore fishermen?
In another field, Holland and Germany import more than $1 million worth of eels annually from the United States. Eels breed in the ocean and they come up our rivers to lay their eggs. What steps have been taken to improve and develop a Canadian eeling industry for export to Europe where they are smoked and considered a delicacy?
Finally, I would like to know-and this is under the minister's responsibility-what progress has been made in opening up the Canadian swordfish market in the United States. Now that an acceptable level of mercury in swordfish has been established in the United States, swordfish catches are showing up on the docks of Gloucester, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida. This is a multimillion dollar industry. I recently held discussions with the Japanese ambassador concerning the potential for swordfish in his country.
