speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks are largely confined to Part VII, having to do with the National Research Council. According to the 1977-78 report of the president, the National Research Council is to "undertake, assist or promote scientific and engineering research to further Canada's economic and social development".
Since 1917 the NRC has been the premier research agency in Canada. The government has modified the functions and altered some objectives of the NRC in recent years in its effort to co-ordinate scientific effort in Canada. It is beyond question that the policies of the government have greatly altered the operation of the NRC. It is certainly questionable whether the co-ordination of the Canadian science effort has been effective. Until recently, NRC had three operations programs, namely the engineering and natural sciences research program, the scientific and technical information program, and the scholarships and grants in aid of research program.
In 1974-75 the principal research activities of the NRC were modified so that the highest priorities were accorded to the following two activities. Firstly, top priority was given to research on long-term projects of national concern. This research is directed toward the solution of problems in such areas as energy, food, transportation, building and construction. Second priority was assigned to research in direct support of industrial innovation and development. This category includes research on promising areas of new technology, effective methods of technology transferred to industry and technical and financial assistance to industry to carry out specific research and development projects to the point of industrial innovation.
In 1977-78 technology transfer and utilization of research results was accorded a separate priority status reflecting the growing concern for the dismal state of Canada's secondary manufacturing industries and the low level of innovative high technology industry in this country.
It is important to note, however, that the NRC has not abandoned its basic and exploratory research which composes
Government Organization
about 25 per cent of its intramural research effort, a field that has won world-wide respect for the council.
In 1972, the special Senate Committee on Science Policy recommended that the NRC be transformed into "an academy devoting all its activities to basic research and long-term applied research with no specific objective, that most of the intramural basic research be concentrated in this institution, and that a substantial portion of its work be performed at the request of government agencies and private firms on a fee basis."
At the same time, the granting function of the NRC would be given to a "new foundation for the physical sciences". This proposal has been converted into reality with the creation by parliament in 1977 of the natural sciences and engineering research council. Beginning in 1977-78, NSERC has assumed the administration and operation of the NRC's program of scholarships and grants in aid of research in the natural sciences and engineering.
The Senate committee also envisaged the creation of a new institution to be called the Canadian Industrial Laboratories Corporation, primarily to carry out intramural research and development programs designed to serve the needs of manufacturing industries. To date the government has not acted on this proposal.
Finally, the Ministry of State for Science and Technology was intended by the science committee to be the central government ministry charged with the task of reviewing and assessing the proposed science programs of the other departments and agencies of the federal government. To date, the Ministry of State for Science and Technology has not been able to discharge this simple duty.
I want to consider for a moment the effect of the creation of the NSERC and the loss of this granting function by the NRC. In the past the NRC has spun off certain major functions as these have grown to independent status of their own. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the Defence Research Board and the Medical Research Council are cases in point. These three organizations are different in nature from the NRC's granting function. To refer back to the National Research Council of Canada report of the president, 1977-78, at page 18, Dr. Schneider comments:
The separation of the university grants function which has been one of the cornerstones of NRC's broader science role in Canada represents a more fundamental change. In fact, the development and nurturing of scientific research in Canada and the provision of the necessary infrastructure for science has been an ongoing NRC responsibility since its was established some 62 years ago. There is no doubt that the interaction with the university sector which this role engendered has been highly beneficial to NRC in carrying out its own research mission, and the close contact it has had with all three sectors, university, industry and government, has greatly facilitated the co-ordination of research programs in Canada. In order to retain some of these advantages in future, it will be essential for NRC to endeavour to maintain active liaison with a new council and the university sector.
In the future, because of the creation of the NSERC the role of the NRC will be less involved in the general development of science in Canada, particularly at the university level. Rather, NRC's future role will be more mission oriented and, according to the same report:

March 8, 1979
Government Organization
... largely centred around its laboratory programs together with extramural research projects strongly coupled so as to reinforce, extend or exploit laboratory programs. Additionally special emphasis will continue to be given to promoting industrial research and development and to supporting promising research projects in industry.
The granting function represented a major program for NRC, amounting to almost $110 million in 1978-79. Whether the separation of the two bodies will affect the relationship between NRC and the university basic research program remains to be seen. In addition to the fear that the creation of the NSERC will have a detrimental effect on the general development of science in Canada is the concern that the appointment of a non-scientist to the presidency of the new council has not been well received by the scientific community.
The formation of a Canadian industrial laboratories corporation proposed by the special Senate committee has not been accomplished. The committee felt that CILC was necessary because the NRC could not, in the committee's view, excel in the fields of basic research and industrial research. It is perhaps appropriate to question the accuracy of this conclusion since NRC has the right to claim considerable success in both areas. During the last five years 80 patents resulted from research carried out in NRC laboratories and, of these, 42 have thus far been successfully licensed to industries in Canada.
Under NRC's industrial research assistance program 255 projects were supported during 1977-78 for a total value of $15.6 million, which supported 744 research scientists and 507 technicians on industrial research projects. As a partial measure of benefits arriving from successful completion of IRAP projects, a sample survey of ten companies showed that previous IRAP support of $3,619 million subsequently led to the creation of 410 new permanent jobs in these industries or one job per $8,800 of IRAP funds invested. These figures do not include indirect employment in associated construction, subcontracts and services. Contracts completed, currently in place and under negotiation under NRC's program for industry laboratory projects, PILP, which will cost approximately $25 million are projected to give rise to about $1.5 billion in product sales and about 3,000 jobs.
In addition, the NRC claims that it has established an effective program of technology transfer to industry and that it also has an effective publication and technical information transfer capability. These propositions are demonstrated in the report of the NRC president which I quoted earlier and are illustrated at page 12.
I suggest that this clearly demonstrates the tremendous effectiveness that research and development can have on developing industrial production and marketing capability and creating good jobs in Canada for Canadians. It is my feeling that the creation of the CILC as a spin-off of the NRC is now due and that the specialization we require in this field will be a dynamic to improve Canada's research and development capability in years to come.

Finally, we have to consider the performance of MOSST. With the partial dismantlement of the NRC by the removal of its granting function to the NSERC, Canadian science, in the view of some, no longer has institutional leadership. Certainly, NRC exercised leadership over many years. It is abundantly clear that MOSST does not exercise leadership in science mainly because it has no control over the science program of other federal departments and agencies. Also, the rapid turnover in ministers has inhibited the development of a strong voice in cabinet. One is left to conclude that the government has not effected a comprehensive science policy for Canada. Granted, some of the recommendations of the Senate science committee have been enacted, the NSERC and MOSST, but other recommendations have not been pursued.
Caught in the middle, the NRC has lost its major function as a central power in Canadian science, but no other body has been established to pick up the mantle. It appears to be a question of incomplete planning and inappropriate half actions. In the field of science Canada has lost more in reorganization that it has gained.
Canada's research and development effort is dismal compared with that of other industrialized nations. At present Canada's annual gross expenditure on research and development stands at about .92 per cent of gross national product. In 1970 the figure was 1.21 per cent. In 1975 when Canada's gross expenditure on research and development was 1 per cent, comparable figures for the other nations were: United States, 2.35 per cent; Germany, 2.16 per cent; Japan, 2 per cent; France, 1.86 per cent; Sweden, 1.59 per cent. From 1970 to 1978 the real value of federal government research and development expenditures measured in constant dollars declined, although current dollar expenditures rose each year. Further, regarding the federal government's research and development effort as measured by the ratio of total government research and development, total government spending declined steadily from 3.55 per cent in 1970 to 2.02 per cent in 1976. In 1977-78 there was a slight recovery, with the level on effort measuring 2.1 per cent in 1978.
By the most objective measurements, then, it must be concluded that the present government has not been notably outstanding in its support of science and technology. What is particularly ironic in this situation is the fact that few countries, particularly in the last decade, have devoted as much study, analysis and creative energy to science policy as Canada has.
In 1978 the government made some serious attempts to stimulate research and development both through increased federal funding and through tax incentives. A major goal announced by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) in June was an increase in gross expenditure for research and development to 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product-not gross national product, as reported by many observers and commentators-by 1983. Critics pointed out that to attain this goal, research and development expenditures in industry would have to grow by an average 19 per cent each year and government and university expenditures by 12 per
March 8, 1979

cent or 13 per cent annually. These were seen as possibly unrealistic targets, and it was suggested by some that the total package of incentives announced in June of 1978 was motivated, at least in part, by the anticipated federal election.
In August of 1978, however, the government launched an austerity drive and announced plans to reduce federal spending. Science and technology, including various research and development programs, were affected in some areas. The government proposed to reduce the fisheries program by closing down the main Halifax laboratories and cutting back on the work done at facilities in Vancouver, Winnipeg, St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and St. John's, Newfoundland. The purpose of the cuts was to effect a $2 million saving in the federal budget.
At the same time the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) proposed to eliminate the Petawawa forest experimental station north of Ottawa, a 60-year old enterprise which represents a $100 million Canadian investment in forestry research. The Globe and Mail described the action as being initiated "for the sake of a paltry cut in government spending which is in fact not a cut at all but a bookkeeping exercise to scrape up funds for other spending programs". A loud public outcry ultimately persuaded the government to reconsider its decision.
Agriculture Canada announced at the same time that the Canfarm program, a computer based financial management service to farmers, would be closed out. The program also had a significant research component, particularly in the field of farm management, but also in communications and business administration. The net saving was set at $5.5 million.
Then in his budget speech on November 16, 1978 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced new tax incentives for industries performing research and development.
The picture which emerges over the past year is rather confusing. On the one hand, the government announces increased funding and tax incentives to stimulate Canadian research and development; on the other hand, it abruptly terminates important government research programs. The Globe and Mail commented on the confusing activities of the government in the following way:
If science and technology of which research is the cutting edge are important enough to have a minister of their own they are surely important enough to have a policy of their own. But the manner in which they are left scattered in shreds and patches, $2 million here, $5.5 million there to be cut at the whim of any minister or any department makes it evident that the only policy to which they are subject is that of short-term opportunism and that the only minister responsible for defending them would rather keep his portfolio than fight for it.
A prophetic comment! The minister was promoted. It is at least arguable that the present government, although it has belatedly recognized the importance of research and development both in industry and elsewhere, has not yet evolved an effective and coherent national science policy.
Basic to an effective research and development effort in secondary manufacturing is a national industrial policy. Canada's industrial research and development effort is strangely out of step in the industrialized world in which Canadian products
Government Organization
must compete. The business sector in Canada provides only about one third of research and development expenditures, compared with figures of 40 per cent to 50 per cent for most industrialized countries.
Further, the business sector in Canada performs about 40 per cent of R and D compared to 50 to 65 per cent for business sectors in most advanced countries. In Canada also, for every scientist and engineer engaged in R and D in the government sector there is slightly more than one in the business sector. In 1975 the ratio was actually about 1.2, and 30 per cent of the national scientific and engineering manpower was in universities. In contrast, in the United States, Japan, Germany and Sweden there are approximately five scientists and engineers in the business sector to every one in government or industry.
A factor of major importance in industrial R and D is a very high proportion of foreign ownership of Canadian secondary manufacturing industry. In June of 1978 the Financial Post quoted a science ministry official as stating that Canadian owned firms do proportionately more R and D than do foreign subsidiaries. Thus, until a coherent and effective industrial and foreign investment policy is put in place in Canada it is illogical to expect that effective R and D and significant innovative high technology industry will be developed in Canada.
The forest industry by any standard is a major enterprise in Canada contributing $6 billion to a favourable balance of trade and providing direct or indirect employment for nearly one million people. The industry is in trouble, however, because Canada's share of world markets for forest products has declined over the past 20 years from 31 per cent to 19 per cent, while the United States share has increased from less than 9 per cent to more than 12 per cent. Canada has 13 per cent of the world's soft wood resources but produces only 11 per cent of the world's harvest in soft woods. In contrast, the United States with only 11 per cent of the same resource harvests 22 per cent of the world's total. General productivity in the Canadian wood products industry is about 15 per cent less than in the United States. As a specific example, British Columbia saw mills recovered 25 per cent less lumber from a given log volume than mills in the United States Pacific northwest.
The present state of forest products research and development in Canada is lagging as it is in most areas. But the situation in forestry may be worse than the national average. Federally funded R and D in Canada is about $7 million as compared to $14 million in the United States. Industrially funded R and D in Canada is only $20 million compared to $180 million in the United States. Among the 20 leading industrial sectors in Canada, wood processing ranks last in R and D expenditures.
The Canadian forestry service is only poorly supported by the federal government. Although forestry once enjoyed the status of a separate department, the federal effort has been consistently reduced over the years. In the last decade the

March 8, 1979
Government Organization
Canadian forest service has lost more than 50 per cent of its man-years, a time period when significant manpower growth has occurred in almost every other area of the federal public service. The budget of the Canada forest service is only one quarter that of the federal science and technology expenditures for fisheries, energy, mines and resources, and agriculture. Forestry is noted to contribute $6 billion to Canada's trade balance, which is comparable to the net contribution of fuels and minerals and much greater than the $1 billion created by agriculture and the $0.3 billion from fisheries.
The budget of the Canada forest service will be slashed by a further $5.3 million, or 15 per cent, in 1979. Both the eastern and western forest products laboratories are to be handed over to the private sector and will face an effective budget cut of more than 45 per cent as of April 1, 1979.
Again, the government actions in cutting forestry in R and D is puzzling, considering the stated intention to stimulate industrial related R and D in Canada. The forest enterprise is already seriously underfinanced at the federal level and the proposed cuts can hardly be justified. One might suggest that these moves represent another symptom of the lack of a coherent federal science policy.
Consider the recent government program to assist in the modernization of our pulp and paper industry over the next three years. It has a pleasant sound but the sound is distorted when we look at the government's performance. On June 1 of last year the government earmarked $2 million for the creation of five regional university based industrial research innovation centres, to be spent over the next five years in consultation with the provinces. Where are they? They are non-existent.
The centres of excellence was another excellent program announced last June. The province of New Brunswick in good faith proposed a forestry complex for the University of New Brunswick to assist the forest industry which is so important to Atlantic Canada. Last fall I asked the minister of science when the announcements would be made and he indicated that many interesting proposals have been received and were being reviewed; and, Mr. Speaker, they are still being reviewed. Where are they?
Another proposal to expand the NRC's program of industry laboratory projects is an excellent development but there is a dearth of information regarding its implementation. There is also great disappointment that it was not extended to include university laboratories. The research experience that inhouse university scientists or engineers have must be combined to assist the industrial development of marketable products. I believe too that Canada's scientific and technological associations are capable of making a major contribution in the process of developing the appropriate marketing and management skills necessary to effect transfer of technology to the private sector.
I remain deeply concerned that the government has not yet devised a long-term policy for the funding of university based scientific research. Three to five-year budget projections for the granting councils updated annually would confer a much

needed stability to the Canadian university research effort and eliminate cost-ineffective on and off funding planning.
The government's procurement policy announced last June is still not before us and a new and important role for FIRA is still mystery. The government announced new programs which are not implemented, dismantled old programs, does complete about-faces in terms of industrial incentives for research and development, and sets small national goals which it seems to hope to achieve by some form of magic or levitation. Our science policy seems comparable to the man who jumped on a horse and drove off in all directions. In real terms we are making a great effort and going nowhere.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for copies of all correspondence, notes, minutes of meetings and other communications relating to the decentralization of the Department of Veterans Affairs to the province of Prince Edward Island.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have spoken on this motion on previous occasions and will not repeat my comments, which are already on the record. Suffice it to say that I have asked for these papers because concerns are still being expressed about the move of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Prince Edward Island.
Let me put on the record that I am not speaking against decentralization but only hoping that enough information can be produced to convince everyone that the move is a wise one. In that regard, all I want to do this afternoon is to put on the record some of the latest concerns that have been expressed, and I will do that by reading an extract from a letter which has been sent to me, and possibly to other members of the House, dated February 2 from the Royal Canadian Legion. It reads in part:
The Royal Canadian Legion is convinced that the inclusion of the Canadian Pension Commission in the move of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Prince Edward Island is a grave error. We had serious reservations in 1976 when the decentralization plan was first announced and told the minister so. We believed then and we do so even more strongly today that it would be impossible to move the commission without serious impairment of that organization's ability to serve disability pensioners, prospective pensioners and their dependants.
We are in sympathy with the plan to create jobs in Prince Edward Island, but not at the expense of disabled war veterans.
March 8, 1979

In the attachment to the letter one can read as follows:
The Royal Canadian Legion opposes this move for it is convinced, after careful evaluation of the position, that such a move will have a very harmful effect on the commission's ability to serve veterans. It is the Legion's view that it will impair efficiency, reduce productivity and involve substantial delays in adjudication for a period of three to five years.
The commission employs many specialists, both in medical and other categories. These people are vital to the maintenance of a fair and efficient adjudicating process. It takes years of experience and training as members of the commission staff before the majority are proficient to a point where they can process pension claims according to the high standards which we have come to expect as proper. For example, it normally takes two years or so for a doctor to be fully versed in the specialized pension work. The number of such specialists who have indicated that they would be willing to move to Prince Edward Island is pitifully small. For example, four doctors on the medical advisory staff out of twenty-five seem likely to move!
Many of the medical/clerical specialists who now work for the commission are married women whose family ties will make it impossible for them to move to Prince Edward Island. It is not easy to recruit suitable people for this work in Ottawa, where there is a considerable pool of prospective candidates. We believe it would be very difficult to recruit and train people for employment in Prince Edward Island, without a serious deterioration in the speed of processing claims, and the standards of adjudication.
A percentage of pension claims has to be processed in French. The reluctance of French-speaking persons to move from the province of Quebec to Ottawa is a known fact. This is so despite excellent educational and cultural activities in the French tongue which the Ottawa area can provide. We believe that the task of recruiting properly trained French-speaking people to fulfil the commission's requirements in Charlottetown will be a difficult one.
The relative isolation of Charlottetown also gives cause for concern. Despite official claims to the contrary, this cannot help but make for delays. As is well known, these occur now, despite the fact that Ottawa is more or less in the centre of things. With the exception of entitlement boards, almost all of the commission's business is transacted by correspondence. Eight per cent only of the veteran population lives in the Atlantic region, within easy reach of Charlottetown.
The isolation of Charlottetown will also complicate the travel arrangements of the pension commissioners who must move around the country to hold personal hearings. The extra travel time required for journeys to western Canada will mean a reduction in the number of cases to be heard each trip, unless travel on Saturdays and Sundays becomes the norm.
The Royal Canadian Legion has continued to press for the retention of the Pension Commission in Ottawa since the move was first announced.
I put those comments of the Royal Canadian Legion on the record as I think they express these concerns in just as good terms as possibly I could use. I have asked for the documentation and papers supporting the move on the assumption the department has already looked into these questions. I should like to know what answers it came up with, and that is why I have asked for the production of these papers. I think this recent letter of just last month from the Royal Canadian Legion is a clear indication of the continuing concerns that have been expressed by many groups, and it is for that reason I ask again that there be more disclosure of the investigation carried out prior to the decision to make this move.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main object of this bill is to exempt certain practices of shipping conferences from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. In anticipation of the expiry of legislation currently in force this year, the government has considered the question whether or not to continue to exempt conferences from the provision of the act. The government has concluded that conferences continue to serve the public interest in providing stable services for Canadian shippers at reasonable cost. This was also the almost unanimous view of the private sector as reflected in the responses to inquiries carried out last year by the Canadian Transport Commission in connection with the review of the effectiveness of the current legislation.
The main features of the present legislation have been retained in Bill S-6. There are, however, a number of significant changes designed, for the most part, to ensure the protection of Canadian interests, particularly Canada shippers who make use of conference services.
Bill S-6 was given very thorough examination in the other place. Its standing committee on transport and communications met on numerous occasions and received submissions from various groups representing conferences and shippers. While the carriers and shippers differed on a number of aspects of the bill, all were in favour of continuing to exempt conferences from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. Moreover, I think it became clear during the course of the discussions that Bill S-6 represents a reasonable compromise between the requirements of the conferences on the one hand and shippers on the other. Minor amendments designed to provide clarification of some clauses of the bill were adopted in the other place, and I can now recommend Bill S-6 to the House and request its early passage.

subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT, 1979 MEASURE TO EXEMPT CERTAIN PRACTICES FROM PROVISIONS OF COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been mentioned already, Bill S-6 received quite an exhaustive review in the other place. As has also been mentioned, basically the bill would extend the provisions of legislation enacted in the early 1970s which will expire at the end of this month. The bill would provide exemptions with regard to certain practices of shipping conferences operating in Canada and outside Canada. The exemptions to which I refer are in relation to the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act under several different circumstances.
In general terms I suspect that this bill is probably essential at this time in the sense that shipping conferences are operating now. We deal in an international shipping situation, and it would be difficult for Canada to change the system without some massive restructuring of our own shipping system. However, that does not alter the fact that the whole principle of encouraging this type of monopolistic tendency in the shipping industry is not good for Canada, the Canadian consumer or the Canadian shipping industry, what little shipping industry
Shipping
there is left in Canada. This debate opens up the broad question of whether conferences in this sense are good or bad for shipping, the shipping industry, and the economy of Canada.
Shipping conferences are associations of shipping lines. Basically, they are cartels. Bill S-6 would extend the legality of the cartels which have been operating in Canada for some time now. The operations of these conferences in Canada would be illegal except for this bill and, of course, its predecessor act.
It is necessary to look at the consequences of this type of activity in the shipping industry. Because of the operation of shipping conferences, shipping rates are not set by the market forces of supply and demand in general terms but end up being set on the basis of what the market will bear. This means that in Canada, since there is no competition, or very little, in international shipping, we have higher rates and lower rates, depending on the type of goods shipped. There is a tendency toward price discrimination in Canadian shipping. There are higher rates for high value and low weight goods and lower rates for low value and high weight goods. This acts to the detriment of Canadian consumers.
A justification for restraint upon competition in the shipping industry, other than the fact that this is the way it has always been and this is the way the world runs in general terms, is that it maintains the health of merchant marines. It also maintains regular and frequent cargo services and creates-it is alleged-stable rates in the system.
The first of these justifications just does not apply to Canada because we do not have a merchant marine. It has been the policy of this government and of previous governments to allow our merchant marine to deteriorate to the point where it does not exist any more.
The operation of conferences may give us stable rates in the shipping industry, but the prices, while they may be stable, are still too high. A study, commissioned by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, by the institute for policy analysis at the University of Toronto came to the conclusion that the high prices in this area are an excessive price to pay for any alleged advantages of a healthy liner trade. We do not even have one in Canada right now and we still have to pay the price. That institute and that study, which was released not too long ago, recommend change and reform in the system immediately. This bill continues the recent trends in world shipping of decreasing and lessening competition in the industry, which has not been good for Canada mainly because we do not have an industry operating in the field.
Generally speaking, conferences augment their power and exercise their power through discriminatory pricing, which has tended to favour exports over imports in Canada recently. This may be good in terms of balance of payment, but in the long run leads to certain misallocation of resources and a high cost to consumers. Also, they operate by means of patronage agreements to force shippers to use only certain lines or routes. The competition between conferences even is limited. There

March 8, 1979
Shipping
are some 50 conferences operating out of Canada on international routes, but on essentially heavily used routes like the north Atlantic there is such a great overlapping membership among these several conferences that there is very little effective competition among them.
Other countries have attempted to control the power of these conferences in various ways, through regulation and so on, where the conferences' activities are most obviously in conflict with the public interest, but in general the effects of regulation have been negligible in terms of positive effects upon the economic welfare. So with the experience of other countries as a guide, it seems pointless for Canada to attempt regulation of conferences in conjunction with this type of bill in order to minimize their most objectionable points. But then neither should we make their activities legal when our whole economic tradition dictates that we should be doing just the opposite, that is, increasing competition.
Canada has no merchant marine, as I mentioned before, and in two ways this would, or should, dictate that we not allow conferences such leeway in our economy. Without a merchant marine we have no leverage in the shipping industry to control the adverse effect of the conference operations. As well, there is no benefit to Canada as a result of the high rates which result from conferences. High rates in another country might encourage the development or continuance of a merchant marine and its healthy operation; in Canada that factor does not exist because we do not have a merchant marine.
However, there is a problem, and that is why I suggest at this time that, in spite of my opposition to the bill, it might be difficult to make conferences totally subject to the Combines Investigation Act, because most conferences or most lines operating in Canada also belong to conferences operating out of the United States and it would be very difficult to prove collusion or some other action contrary to the Combines Investigation Act, where, in most cases, it would only be a passive agreement between conferences or member lines of conferences. But in spite of those difficulties we should not be encouraging such practices as price discrimination, and perhaps we could specifically prohibit them if we did not allow the legalization of the conferences in this country.
As I mentioned before, one of the main reasons for this bill right now-and the problem 1 have with this bill-is that we do not have a merchant marine. If Canada had a viable merchant marine we could effectively counter the power of conferences on the international scene, and we could effectively gain from the rate structures and the frameworks that are set up by conferences internationally. It is astounding to me that the Canadian government would make a conscious decision as far back as the early 1950s not to foster a merchant marine. At one time, as hon. members are aware, Canada was one of the top countries in the world in the size and power of its merchant marine. Now our sea-going traffic is limited mainly to lake traffic on the Great Lakes in central Canada. For a country that relies as heavily on international trade as does Canada, we should have some control over the way we get our goods to markets and over the way we bring goods from

overseas. The whole problem of shipping conferences is that they operate with little if any direction or control by Canada, and because of the monopolistic tendencies of the conference operations they do us harm economically.
Not only do we not have a merchant marine but we do not require Canadian companies such as CP, which receive many dollars in subsidies and tax referrals, to register their ships in Canada like a good corporate citizen should. The benefits of bringing home these vessels, which are now flying flags of convenience like Bermuda but are beneficially owned in Canada, would be great. It would give us a merchant marine under Canadian control to counter the power of the conferences internationally. It would provide jobs and employment at home rather than in foreign countries which fly flags of convenience, it would subject the ships to greater Canadian regulation in a great many fields, including working conditions, and finally, it would benefit consumers by providing a competitive Canadian presence in world shipping.
This bill would not be perceived to be so necessary or so objectionable if Canada had its own merchant marine, and I suggest it is incumbent on this government to begin developing one now rather than pursue a conscious policy which is going in the opposite direction. Also, I suggest that this government should encourage, and perhaps require companies like CP, Federal Commerce and Irving Oil, to register their ships in Canada, thereby employing Canadians and making them subject to Canadian law. It is important to bring some democracy and competition back to the market place in the shipping industry so that Canadian workers and consumers will benefit.
As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, at this time, without some drastic reorganization of the Canadian shipping industry structure, it is probably a little impractical for the government not to pass this bill at present. But in principle we are opposed to it because of the reasons I have outlined, that it decreases and restrains competition in the industry, thereby bringing less benefits and greater costs to Canadian consumers, Canadian workers, and the Canadian industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dennis Dawson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT, 1979 MEASURE TO EXEMPT CERTAIN PRACTICES FROM PROVISIONS OF COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main object of this bill is to exempt certain practices of the shipping conferences from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act.
Let me provide some background, Mr. Speaker. Shipping conferences are associations or groups of shipping lines serving the same route or area that act together to set rates and other conditions under which they will carry goods. These associations or conferences exist in what is known as liner sectors, that is, among companies operating between fixed points on a regularly scheduled basis. Moreover, conferences exist primarily in the carriage of general cargo rather than in the dry or wet bulk trade, such as the shipment of wheat or oil. Conferences carry about 10 per cent of the Canadian exports in tonnage terms but considerably more in dollar terms since much of their business consists of higher value goods.
There are about 50 conferences serving Canada at the present time, each consisting of two or more members and
March 8, 1979

each serving a particular trade, such as exports from Canada, the United Kingdom, Scandinavia or Japan, with separate conferences covering the inbound trade.
The shipping lines making up any given conference typically adopt an agreement which governs their membership voting procedures and other aspects of their relationship. They maintain a permanent office or offices, and meet from time to time to agree on rates for various commodities, or to discuss other matters in relation to the operation of the conferences. While conference members normally agree on rates, at least for most commodities, typically they also compete with each other for business on the basis of such factors as service or delivery times. In many trades they also are in competition with other lines that are not members of that conference, or for certain high value products with the airlines.
The conference system is not new, nor is it unique to Canada. Liner operators have been operating in conferences for more than 100 years, and are active in most parts of the world. Since their origins in the 1870s, conferences have been subject to analysis and discussion, both internationally and in Canada. In this country, for example, there have been several investigations into conference activities, the first of which was in 1913. The most extensive inquiry was that carried out by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission which concluded, in a 1965 report, that conferences operate as cartels, contrary to the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, but that the public interest would not be served by the excessive rate and service instability that might result if shipping conferences were not permitted to exist. It was the report of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission that led to the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, which came into force on April 1, 1971, and which will expire on March 31 this year.
The act that is currently in effect sets out a number of conference practices, such as the common setting of rates, that are exempted from the Combines Investigation Act. At the same time it sets out other practices, such as the use of deferred rebates, that are not exempted from the act, or in other words, practices that are not permitted. The act also requires conferences to file copies of conference agreements, memberships, tariffs, etc. with the Canadian Transport Commission so that they are accessible to the public. This is the framework of the legislation currently in force, allowing conferences to operate in Canadian trades subject to clearly established ground rules.
In anticipation of the expiry of legislation currently in force this year, the government has considered the question of whether or not to continue to exempt conferences from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. The government has concluded that conferences continue to serve the public interest, in providing stable services for Canadian shippers at reasonable cost. This also was the almost unanimous view of the private sector, as reflected in responses to an inquiry carried out last year by the Canadian Transport Commission
Shipping
in connection with a review of the effectiveness of the current legislation.
The main features of the present legislation have been retained in Bill S-6. There are, however, a number of significant changes, designed for the most part to ensure the protection of Canadian interests, particularly Canadian shippers who make use of conference services.
Clause 8, which spells out filing requirements, ensures that changes to tariffs and other conference documents will be accessible to shippers and other interested groups on the date on which they come into effect, rather than 30 days after the date of their adoption, as in the current legislation.
Clauses 13 and 14 require conference members to make copies of all conference documents available for inspection or purchase at an office or agency in the region of Canada where they operate, and to make copies of current tariffs available for inspection at all members' principal offices or agencies in Canada. This would provide shippers with easier access to relevant information since at the present time the conferences are required only to file this information with the Canadian Transport Commission.
Clause 15 requires members of conferences operating from Canada to meet with designated shipper groups, when reasonably requested to do so, and to provide the shipper group with information sufficient for the satisfactory conduct of the meeting. This section is designed to ensure that such conferences meet with Canadian shippers to discuss problems of mutual interest and to ensure that shippers are provided with information on which they can judge conference actions, such as proposed rate increases.
While it is hoped that any additional information can be obtained voluntarily, clause 16 empowers the governor in council to make regulations requiring members of a conference to provide information necessary to enable the commission effectively to supervise their activities. The government appreciates the sensitivity of this question of information, but is of the view that clause 16 contains adequate and appropriate safeguards to protect the legitimate interests of various members.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, clause 23 provides for the legislation to expire after five years, with provision for extension by proclamation for periods not exceeding five years.
Bill S-6 was given very thorough examination in the other place. Its standing committee on transport and communications met on numerous occasions, and received submissions from various groups representing conferences and shippers. While the carriers and shippers differed on a number of aspects of the bill, all were in favour of continuing to exempt conferences from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. Moreover, I think it became clear during the course of the discussion that Bill S-6 represents a reasonable compromise between the requirements of the conferences on the one hand, and of the shippers on the other.
Minor amendments designed to provide clarification of some clauses of the bill were adopted in the other place, and I think

subtopic: POST OFFICE-OVERNIGHT INTERCITY COURIER SERVICE-ALLEGED SECRECY RESPECTING PROGRAM
POST OFFICE-OVERNIGHT INTERCITY COURIER SERVICE-ALLEGED SECRECY RESPECTING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 2 I questioned the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamon-tagne) about the new overnight courier service which it was rumoured had been launched by the Post Office Department.

March 8, 1979

There has been a veil of secrecy surrounding this service. The rumour was circulating following the somewhat embarrassing information revealed in the House that the Post Office Department has phased out this so-called assured mail service notwithstanding the expenditure of something like $1.5 million to provide special boxes and facilities of that kind to launch this now phased out program of assured mail.
It became necessary to ask the question then because it was impossible to get information from the department. Unfortunately this is a pattern that has been adopted by the Post Office increasingly in recent years. It has been surrounded by a sea of troubles, frequent changes of postmasters general, trouble with its mechanization program, increasing labour-management difficulties resulting in frequent strikes, and, of course, the inevitable result is the loss of business to private couriers.
The Postmaster General replied to my inquiry in rather enigmatic terms. He says this as reported at page 3763 of Hansard for March 2, 1979:
It seems the hon. member is referring to our new service which is called Priority Post. It was devised to give to certain customers under contract a mail service comparable to that of any private enterprise competing with us at the moment. We could promote it, in a way, without publicity; the reason we have not publicized it is that we wanted to make sure that the operation was a success, that it was self-sufficient and that undertaking this new venture would not lead to a requirement for more money from taxpayers.
He goes on to say:
There is nothing secret about it. It is just a question of good management on the part of the Post Office.
It really is quite secret. I was amazed in light of what the Postmaster General said that the Post Office Department had not been shouting from the rooftops about this overnight courier service. The best way, and this has always been a custom in this House as you well know, Mr. Speaker, when new programs of this kind are announced, is that they are announced in the House of Commons and members of parliament have a chance to respond. The public is informed, and the information should result in a favourable response from potential users of a new service of this kind.
Unfortunately, as I have said, the Post Office has developed an inferiority complex. It has become paranoid almost to the point where it is shrouding itself in a veil of secrecy. It refuses to table reports that would be helpful in resolving Post Office difficulties. There is suspicion and confrontation between management and labour rather than consultation and co-operation. This attitude even extends to the proposed Crown corporation legislation where the Post Office is surreptitiously attempting to extend its monopoly by using phrases such as "the transfer of goods" instead of transfer of parcels, and "the transmission of messages" rather than the conveyance of mail, which suggests it wants to move into the electronic transmission business. It spends great sums of money in fighting courier services, such as UPS, rather than providing the superior service which would compete easily with private couriers if the Post Office could only get its act together.
Adjournment Debate
The point in raising this matter tonight is to restore confidence in the Post Office. Canada used to have the best postal service in the world. It was open and accessible to all Canadians. Members on this side of the House still believe that the Post Office is capable of recovering its morale and its efficiency. We believe it should be open and honest with the public if it is providing this service, instead of keeping it close to the chest. Let the public know that overnight courier service is available. Then they will recover the business and will increase their revenues in this manner rather than having to go to the regular periodic increases in rates which have occurred with frequency over the last three years. Inevitably when rates are increased one must face the prospect of losing business to competitors.
I would hope that when the parliamentary secretary replies he will be forthcoming to the House, that he will tell us without equivocation that the service is the best available, and let the customers know that the Post Office is trying to provide the service it is capable of providing rather than hiding its light under a bushel.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-OVERNIGHT INTERCITY COURIER SERVICE-ALLEGED SECRECY RESPECTING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) for accommodating my schedule this evening by allowing this question to be dealt with first in the adjournment debate.
I think I can give the assurances to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) that he wanted in terms of explaining Priority Post. When I have concluded my remarks I will give him a promotional piece of literature which the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) signed for his edification. I can really only repeat the minister's answer that was given in the House the other day. I quote from Hansard:
It was devised to give to certain customers under contract a mail service comparable to that of any private enterprise competing with us at the moment. We could promote it, in a way, without publicity; the reason we have not publicized it is that we wanted to make sure that the operation was a success, that it was self-sufficient and that undertaking this new venture would not lead to a requirement for more money from taxpayers.
To say that we have kept the service a secret is somewhat inaccurate. How can a service operate if we keep it a secret? How could we have contacted over 500 business firms and induced them to try a secret service? We have had coloured brochures, like the one I have in my hand, specially coloured bags, training programs, interval instructions and reports to postal employees. How could this have been done if it had been our desire to keep the service secret?
Knowing the diligence with which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris pursues his activities as official critic for the Post Office, those of us associated with the Post Office are not so naive as to think for one moment that we could keep something secret from the hon. gentleman. It can be seen that indeed it was not a secret. From past experience we knew perfectly well that the hon. gentleman would pose enough piercing questions often enough to gain us many lines of free

March 8, 1979
Adjournment Debate
publicity across the country. He has done that.We thank him very much for drawing public attention to this very worthwhile service.
What is Priority Post? I am not sure how much time I have left. I could tell the House it is a new service from Canada Post, fundamentally a next day premium mail service between designated places of business. It is only offered on an individual service agreement basis. That means that the Priority Post you buy has been tailored specifically to the needs and schedules of the various businesses. It also means that, in committing itself to an agreed service, Canada Post plans to live up to its end of the bargain.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO REDUCE CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO REDUCE CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the adjournment debate that I join in tonight arises from a question I attempted to put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday dealing with Statistics Canada current account deficit figures that were released at one o'clock yesterday afternoon. Unfortunately the Prime Minister was right out of it yesterday. He must have had a very bad caucus or something because he literally did not understand what I was talking about.
I was talking about the fact that it was revealed yesterday that our current account deficit was $5,261 million for the year 1978. That means we had a record deficit in that year, a record for any year to which you want to compare it. Most important, the fourth quarter of last year was also a record deficit. I think it is unfortunate that the government is attempting to gloss over the extent of the deficit into which it has led this nation. The fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was in this House until a few minutes ago and then left without replying to my remarks this evening shows how little they care about informing this House and the Canadian public concerning this matter.
A deficit of $5,200 million on current account represents 2.2 per cent of the gross national product of this country last year. That is a record deficit, as I have said, and it is a record ratio. When we compare it to the deficit in the United States we find that the U.S. current deficit was $17 billion on a $2,111.2 billion economy. Their ratio was .81 per cent. What is of even greater importance, though, is that in the economic report of the President transmitted to Congress in January of this year the following statement is made:
The United States current account deficit is expected to decline considerably from the levels at the end of 1978, dropping to about an annual rate of $2-$8 billion by the end of 1979.
In short, Canadians have been led into a current account deficit which is almost equal to the anticipated deficit in the United States in the present year. Let us get this into perspective. All OECD countries in 1978 were, in the aggregate, actually in surplus as far as current accounts were concerned. All those countries, put together, were in surplus. We had a deficit of $5.2 billion. Let me put on record the surpluses of

some of those other countries: Japan $20 billion, Germany $6 billion, France $2 billion, Italy had a surplus of $5.5 billion, and the United Kingdom had a deficit of $500 million compared to our deficit of $5.2 billion.
We note that time and again the Government of Canada is borrowing foreign funds. Appearing before a committee of the other place, the governor of the Bank of Canada, speaking on January 24 with regard to foreign borrowing, said we borrow enough money to cover our current account deficit. Then he went on to say, "I certainly do feel the current account deficit is too large now." The governor made that comment when it was anticipated that our current deficit for 1978 would be $4.5 billion. It turned out to be $700 million more than anticipated. Not only have we permitted a record deficit, but it is growing. We find, for example, that in 1973 this country actually had a surplus as far as our trade and services account with the rest of the world was concerned. But in the last five years we have run up an aggregate deficit with the rest of the world of $19,429 million. This means that for every man, woman and child in this country we have gone into debt to the extent of $844.
It has been said that somehow this position will correct itself if we can hold inflation down. But the sad fact is that to the degree this deficit has caused our dollar to collapse, it is causing inflation. It is expected that the CPI figures to be released next week will show on a month over month basis that inflation in February of this year was running approximately 9.4 per cent higher than one year ago. This is an intolerable situation. The government is simply using monetary means, the borrowing of foreign funds, to cover a foreign account deficit instead of using effective fiscal measures to correct the problem to which I have referred.
The whole key to this situation is not to take the current account deficit as a basis and then just try to finance it by foreign borrowing and forcing up our interest rates either to prevent a capital outflow or to stimulate an inflow. The Trudeau government has placed the Bank of Canada in an impossible position because it is asking them to use purely monetary tools to correct a situation which can only be corrected by fiscal steps. A Canadian dollar defence using monetary policy is doomed to failure from the beginning because the government has asked the Bank of Canada to do an impossible job.
When I raised the question yesterday I sincerely hoped that the Prime Minister would rise and say that the government was alarmed, that it felt it could handle this problem by monetary means-foreign borrowing-that it now realizes it has to take more severe fiscal steps, and that it is going to narrow the budgetary deficit which is triple, in relative terms, the deficit with which the Americans are living. If the Prime Minister had said that, I would not be in this debate tonight. However, not only did he refuse to say anything, but commenting on the figures I have referred to, the Minister of Finance said yesterday that this is a problem we have to live with. The hard truth is that this country cannot live with a chronic
March 8, 1979

current account deficit of the magnitude we have been led into by this government. That is why I was hoping we would have received some answers tonight, not from a parliamentary secretary but from the Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alan Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO REDUCE CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that it is blatantly unfair of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) to suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) should be here in this late show to respond to his question. He knows the tradition in this parliament whereby it is completely accepted that parliamentary secretaries respond at this time.
The second point I would like to make is that it is equally blatantly unfair of the hon. member to have anticipated that in the absence of the Minister of Finance yesterday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), having just come into the building at two o'clock, should have been briefed on a release which came out at one o'clock.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO REDUCE CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext: He had it the day before.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO REDUCE CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext:
These points should be borne in mind.
Let me point out that historically Canada's balance of international payments has been characterized by a significant deficit on current account and a surplus on capital transactions. Current account deficits for Canada are neither new-in fact, they are the rule, not the exception-nor are they in themselves a bad thing.
The current account of Canada's balance of payments has registered a deficit in 25 of the past 30 years. As a percentage of gross national product the current account deficit it not out of line with our historical experience. In order to finance high levels of capital formation and enhance economic growth, Canada has traditionally supplemented its domestic savings by recourse to foreign capital markets. Deficits on current account are the necessary counterpart of this.
Nevertheless, under present circumstances the government would view a reduction in Canada's current account deficit as a favourable development. Despite temporary reversals we are optimistic that this will occur. Since the first quarter of 1976 we have experienced a substantial improvement in our merchandise trade account, and we expect further gains. As the House knows, the merchandise trade balance registered a record surplus of $3.5 billion in 1978. The merchandise trade figures for January, which were recently released, showed a merchandise trade surplus of $386 million. Projected on an annual basis, it comes to $4.6 billion. Our competitive position on international markets, which earlier had been a cause for concern, is much improved, and this should exert a positive influence on our current account over the coming quarters.
An additional favourable indicator is the halt in the deterioration in our travel balance. In fact, in the fourth quarter it registered a significant improvement.
The increase in the current account deficit was primarily due to increases in net payments of interest and dividends abroad and a swing in the balance on net transfers from an
Adjournment Debate
inflow of $366 million in 1977 to an outflow of $24 million in 1978. The swing in net transfer payments was almost exclusively due to an increase in official government contributions to non-residents, a large part of which was not a cash outflow.
I should also like to point out that the flow of dividends abroad in the fourth quarter was abnormally large and was associated with the removal of controls on dividends and the expiry of certain deferred tax advantages associated with the tax reforms of 1972.
Additionally, I would like to note that a portion of the increased dividend outflow in the fourth quarter was in the form of stock dividends and was offset by an inflow of direct investment in the capital account. Thus to some degree the deterioration in the current account last year was more apparent than real.

subtopic: ENERGY-INQUIRY WHETHER DREE REPRESENTED IN MARITIME ENERGY CORPORATION
ENERGY-INQUIRY WHETHER DREE REPRESENTED IN MARITIME ENERGY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Maritime Energy Corporation is an excellent vehicle for the development of a full-scale maritime power pool with strong interconnections to the United States and the rest of Canada. The Maritime Energy Corporation can also be an effective development tool for Atlantic Canada if the federal government is prepared to invest money to help this region help itself.
The government has chosen the Department of Regional Economic Expansion as its instrument for development, and I feel strongly that, as such, it should be represented on the Maritime Energy Corporation directorate and work with it and the premiers of the Atlantic provinces in creating a regional development strategy for Atlantic Canada.
The basic cost of energy is dictated by the cost of production, the cost of transmission, the cost of distribution, and the cost of operating the system. Clearly, the cost of production of energy that is used in an interprovincial grid and the cost of transmitting it is an area where the Government of Canada could wisely invest money in the form of a grant to reduce the cost of the end product. The amount of money invested would have a direct effect on the end product and could result in a very low energy cost. By introducing this low cost energy into the maritime power pool, the total cost of energy would necessarily be lowered.
In plants that are capital intensive and produce power from low cost sources such as hydro plants, tidal plants, and to a lesser degree nuclear plants, the elimination of this capital cost by the Government of Canada would be a real investment in the future of the Atlantic provinces.
If the Maritime Energy Corporation proceeds with the Fundy tidal power study and reports favourably on it, the maritime provinces would have in place a massive energy source that would be most attractive to metal and chemical based companies which could well locate on the periphery of such a plant, creating a large number of well paying jobs.

March 8, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Then too, plants building electrical components for the staged development of Fundy might find it very much worth their while to build in that area. The spinoff in service and support industries could be considerable. That is where DREE comes in and that is why DREE should be involved with the Maritime Energy Corporation.
DREE should get away from the idea that its main responsibility is to provide industrial incentives to entrepreneurs who wish to move into the Atlantic area, or to local businessmen who want to expand their present operations, or a series of ad hoc programs providing valuable services, but on a small, piecemeal scale. DREE should be doing more than that. It should be looking at the big jobs crying to be tackled. For example, DREE has done nothing so far about the Fundy tidal power project. It is very convenient for the government, whenever Fundy is seriously mentioned, to be able to pass it off to a study or a commission or a committee, which it knows full well can stall the project another year or another decade. DREE should be brought into these discussions. DREE should be handed the responsibility of correlating these studies. DREE should be given the job to do.
DREE was created to lead the attack on regional disparity. Like Uriah, the Hittite, it was to be thrust into the forefront to battle, there to do or die. But DREE stayed in the background when the big conflicts were raised. It handed out its grants and loans to justify its existence, and failed miserably to take hold of the big projects which the Atlantic provinces have needed for generations. In short, it avoided the massive development undertakings without which the Atlantic provinces will always remain what they are today-the most neglected part of Canada.
Finally, I want to say that I am very pleased to see the Maritime Energy Corporation moving forward. In addition to the financial advantages this corporation can have as a vehicle combining the credit potential of three maritime provinces with the Government of Canada, I see tremendous future planning opportunities for the corporation by utilizing the excellent resources of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission and the Nova Scotia Power Corporation which are already in place. I do not envisage a large or expensive organization, nor need it become another layer of bureaucracy. Instead, I see a vehicle for development which has tremendous potential, and its success depends entirely on the extent to which the Government of Canada is prepared to invest in it and develop Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alan Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ENERGY-INQUIRY WHETHER DREE REPRESENTED IN MARITIME ENERGY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before responding to the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), I should like to place on the record a correction to part of my response earlier to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) who was good enough to draw to my attention that Statistics Canada does indeed record that in the fourth quarter of 1978 there was a further slight deterioration in the travel balance. That reference I made should have been to the month of January, 1979, when there was some significant improvement.
Mr. Speaker, on February 19, 1979, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister_qf State for Science and Technology (Mr. Gillespie) tabled a memorandum of understanding between Canada, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island dealing with the Maritime Energy Corporation.
This memorandum establishes the agreed functions which the corporation would perform, and these may be summarized as follows: (1) Carry out regional planning of electrical generation and transmission for the three maritime provinces; (2) finance, build and operate regional generation and transmission; (3) co-ordinate and dispatch the day to day operation of the maritime electrical system; (4) purchase and sell power over transmission ties external to the region; and (5) engage in research and development.
It has been agreed that the Point Lepreau nuclear unit will be MEC's first major project. Its output will be sold through back-to-back contracts with Canada as an intermediate purchaser. This involvement by Canada in back-to-back contracts ensures a strong credit rating for MEC and should permit borrowing for project financing at reasonable rates.
The provincial utilities and the federal government will contribute equity up to 10 per cent of the Lepreau project cost. In addition, the federal government will provide a performance loan to reduce the impact on revenue requirements of possible performance problems that might seriously reduce Lepreau output. The maximum drawdown will be $200 million.
This agreement promises to provide regional co-operation unique in Canada and will ensure greater stability in electricity price within the maritime region than would have been possible without MEC.
There remains to be worked out the detailed legal agreements to implement the decisions reached and to permit the incorporation of Maritime Energy Corporation under the Canada Corporations Act. The shareholders will exercise their rights under these agreements and provide direction to the officers of the corporation through a board of directors nominated by each of the four parties. Federal representation on the board of directors will likely reflect the interests of several departments, and will undoubtedly take into account the individual contribution which directors can make to the effective operation of the new corporation.
The final structure of the board of directors has not yet been determined. It should be noted, however, that in negotiating the details of this agreement the Department of Finance and DREE have been closely associated with Energy, Mines and Resources. Undoubtedly the interests of all three departments will be taken into consideration in the nomination process for members of the board.
